lines.text: The curtain falls on the final dress rehearsal. This time, it falls for Agathe — and for the truth.
Agathe Moreau did not die of a tired heart. She died because she found the missing costumes, and gave the thief one rehearsal's warning before she told the board.
Somewhere in the theatre, a stagehand finds a small black envelope sealed with a silver anchor. It was never delivered. It was never meant to be.
The Théâtre des Marées smells of dust, greasepaint, and rain from the harbour. The final dress rehearsal is running, and the house is half dark.
Agathe Moreau sits at her sewing table in the wings, mending a gown that is not what it pretends to be. She pours her evening tea. She does not see who has already touched the flask.
By the interval she is gone — and the gown on the dummy is a copy, the original sold months ago to a stranger. Nobody ever asked who held the workshop key.

solve.solutionHTML:
The Final Dress Rehearsal — Solved

Inès Marchand, the seamstress Agathe had mentored like a daughter, had been selling the theatre's original 19th-century costumes — the 1890 gown, the 1912 cloak, the 1924 dress — and replacing them with replicas sewn in the workshop. The money went into her bank account, deposit by deposit, matching her private ledger.

Agathe noticed the wrong stitching, found the sales, and left a voicemail for the board chair: she knew who sold them, and she would tell the board after the final rehearsal. Inès cut aconite from the prop garden that morning, hid the sap-stained gloves behind her sewing box, and — the only person free in the twelve-minute interval, the only person who ever prepared Agathe's tea — put it in the flask.

No single clue convicts her. The ledger proves the theft, the gloves prove the poison, and the camera proves the moment. Together, they leave no one else standing.

suspects.secret: He stopped checking the archive months ago and let Inès work there alone after hours — he trusted her completely.
suspects.trustIntro: Tired, honest, and ashamed. He hands you the voicemail tape himself — the one clue that breaks the case open.
truthList: He did not check the archive for months.
Agathe left a voicemail for the board chair the night before she died.
He was cueing lights during the interval.

suspects.alibi: In the stalls, watching the rehearsal; fifty people saw him there.
lieList: My sister and I never argued about the play.
suspects.motive: A long sibling row over the play's ending — Agathe rewrote his final scene, and he never forgave her for it.
suspects.name: Bastien Moreau
suspects.secret: He plagiarised the play's ending from an unpublished manuscript Agathe had shown him years ago — and Agathe knew.
suspects.trustIntro: Wounded pride in a good coat. He argues about art as if it were blood — because in his family, it is.
truthList: He argued with Agathe about the play's ending.
He was in the stalls when she collapsed.
He did not know about the costume sales.

title: The Final Dress Rehearsal

twists.body: The cleaned-up voicemail changes everything: Agathe had found the missing costumes and knew who sold them — but she never names the seller on the tape. She says she will tell the board 'after the final rehearsal,' giving the thief a whole performance to stop her. Was the killer protecting a secret — or protecting someone else? And if Agathe knew, why did she drink the tea her killer prepared?
twists.title: She Knew — But She Never Named the Seller

twists.body: Confronted, Inès breaks — but not the way you expect. She swears she only meant to make Agathe ill, just ill enough to miss the board meeting, that she misjudged the dose, that Agathe was like a mother to her. The ledger says theft. The gloves say intent. The woman in front of you says accident. The board, not her tears, decides which story is true.
twists.title: She Only Meant to Make Her Ill
